newsitem.title: USA: Weather delays U.S. Mars launch until Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Weather delays U.S. Mars launch until Thursday.

text.p: NASA said it would try again on Thursday to launch the first of three probes bound for Mars this year after bad weather thwarted its first attempt.

Mars Global Surveyor was poised for blast-off at 1:16 p.m. EST (1816 GMT) on Wednesday, but gusty upper level winds halted the countdown with just over one minute to go. Thick cloud and rainshowers at Cape Canaveral Air Station earlier postponed the launch by about an hour.

Officials at the U.S. space agency said they had rescheduled the lift-off attempt for noon EST (1700 GMT) on Thursday, with a second opportunity occuring at 1:05 p.m. EST (1805 GMT). Air Force meteorologists said there was a one-in-five chance the weather would not cooperate.
NASA has until Nov. 25 to get the probe off the launch pad. Trips to Mars are only possible once every 26 months.
NASA officials are eager to get the spacecraft under way because each day of delay increases the probe's fuel consumption, shortening its lifetime at Mars.
"It's very important for us on Mars Global Surveyor to launch at the earliest part of our launch opportunity," said Glenn Cunningham, the mission director.

Mars Global Surveyor was designed and built in record time to replace NASA's $1 billion Mars Observer probe, which spun out of control just days before it was due to enter the planet's orbit in 1993. Surveyor carries copies of five of the seven scientific instruments on its ill-fated predecessor, but at $215 million is much less expensive.

The spacecraft is due to slip into an egg-shapped orbit around Mars in September 1997. It will then lower and round off its orbit by dipping into the Red Planet's thin atmosphere, using its wing-like solar panels as brakes.

From an altitude of 230 miles (365 km) its telephoto camera will see objects on the surface as small as a compact car. By the end of one Martian year -- 687 Earth days -- 99 percent of the planet will have been mapped by Surveyor's electronic eye.
The probe does not carry any instruments that could directly detect evidence of life but it may scout out sites for a future robotic mission to recover samples of rock.

Surveyor is the first of three spacecraft, two U.S. and one Russian, destined for the Red Planet this year. NASA plans to send pairs of spacecraft every 26 months through 2005 but has said it has no firm plans to send people to Mars.
Mars Global Surveyor was being launched amid revelations by scientists of possible ancient life on Mars and plans by two New York auction houses to sell fragments of meteorites from the Red Planet.

One of the auction houses, Guernsey's, estimated that three rocks that range from the size of a grapefruit to the size of a golf ball would sell for as much as $2 million when they go on sale on Nov. 20. Separately, Phillips auction house plans to sell three fragments of meteorites from Mars as part of a natural history auction on Dec. 14.
U.S. geologists announced in August they had found possibly life-related compounds in remains of a Martian meteorite that fell to Earth about 13,000 years ago.
